Thank you for submitting your article "The transcriptional corepressor CTBP-1 acts with the SOX family transcription factor EGL-13 to maintain AIA interneuron cell identity in C. elegans" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers at Review Commons, and the evaluation at eLife has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Piali Sengupta as the Senior Editor.

Based on your manuscript, the reviews and your responses, we invite you to submit a revised version incorporating the revisions as outlined in your response to the reviews. It is possible that the revised paper will require re-review.

When preparing your revisions, please also address the following points. Please note that some of these points were not raised by the previous reviewers but are requested by the editors.

1. The issue of egl-13 expression and possible regulation by CTBP-1 in AIA. This was also raised by the reviewers.

2. Please integrate the work in this manuscript better with previous results regarding mechanisms of AIA specification. In particular, it is important to integrate findings regarding the role of TTX-3 in AIA specification with the observations reported here. Is ttx-3 expression affected in egl-13 and/or ctbp-1 mutants? Does the ectopic marker expression observed in ctbp-1 mutants require ttx-3?

3. Please mutate the predicted binding site (PLNLS motif) of CTBP-1 in EGL-13 and assess effects on gene expression. Ideally, this would be done by gene editing.

4. The editors noted a few figures in the manuscript in which presumably representative images are provided but lack any quantification. Please include detailed quantification of all shown phenotypes.

claims.claim: The gene ctbp-1 encodes the sole C. elegans ortholog of the C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP) family of transcriptional corepressors.
claims.source: Here we report the discovery that the C. elegans gene ctbp-1, which encodes the sole worm ortholog of the C-terminal Binding Protein (CtBP) family of transcriptional corepressors (Turner and Crossley, 2001; Chinnadurai, 2002; Chinnadurai, 2003; Shi et al., 2003; Stankiewicz et al., 2014; Nicholas et al., 2008; Reid et al., 2014; Reid et al., 2015; Sherry et al., 2020), functions to maintain the cell identity of the two AIA interneurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing CtBP family members and by the authors' characterization of ctbp-1 as the worm ortholog.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 is essential for the maintenance of the identities of the two AIA interneurons in C. elegans.
claims.source: Here, we show that the gene ctbp-1, which encodes the transcriptional corepressor C-terminal binding protein-1 (CTBP-1), is essential for the maintenance of the identities of the two AIA interneurons in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing defects in AIA gene expression, morphology, and function in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 is not required for the establishment of the AIA cell fate.
claims.source: ctbp-1 is not required for the establishment of the AIA cell fate but rather functions cell-autonomously and can act in later larval stage and adult worms to maintain proper AIA gene expression, morphology and function.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that L1 ctbp-1 mutants have largely normal AIA characteristics, with defects appearing progressively in later stages.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 functions cell-autonomously in the AIA neurons.
claims.source: ctbp-1 is not required for the establishment of the AIA cell fate but rather functions cell-autonomously and can act in later larval stage and adult worms to maintain proper AIA gene expression, morphology and function.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that AIA-specific expression of ctbp-1 rescues the mutant phenotype.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 can act in later larval stage and adult worms to maintain proper AIA gene expression, morphology and function.
claims.source: ctbp-1 is not required for the establishment of the AIA cell fate but rather functions cell-autonomously and can act in later larval stage and adult worms to maintain proper AIA gene expression, morphology and function.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by heat shock experiments showing that induction of ctbp-1 at the L4 stage can rescue AIA defects in adults.

claims.claim: egl-13 encodes a SOX family transcription factor.
claims.source: From a screen for suppressors of the ctbp-1 mutant phenotype, we identified the gene egl-13, which encodes a SOX family transcription factor.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature and by the authors' identification of egl-13 in their suppressor screen.

claims.claim: egl-13 regulates AIA function and aspects of AIA gene expression, but not AIA morphology.
claims.source: We found that egl-13 regulates AIA function and aspects of AIA gene expression, but not AIA morphology.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that egl-13 mutation suppresses AIA functional defects and some gene expression defects but not morphological defects in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: CTBP-1 maintains AIA cell identity in part by utilizing EGL-13 to repress transcriptional activity in the AIAs.
claims.source: We conclude that the CTBP-1 protein maintains AIA cell identity in part by utilizing EGL-13 to repress transcriptional activity in the AIAs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data, yeast two-hybrid assays showing physical interaction, and suppression of ctbp-1 phenotypes by egl-13 mutation.

claims.claim: Eighteen mutant strains with mutations in ctbp-1 express Pceh-28::gfp in a bilaterally symmetric pair of cells located near the posterior of the C. elegans head.
claims.source: In addition to mutants with an undead M4 sister cell, we isolated 18 mutant strains that express Pceh-28::gfp in a manner uncharacteristic of M4 or its undead sister. These mutants express Pceh-28::gfp in a bilaterally symmetric pair of cells located near the posterior of the C. elegans head, far from both M4 and the single M4 sister cell (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1A showing GFP expression in cells near the posterior head region.

claims.claim: The cells misexpressing Pceh-28::gfp in ctbp-1 mutants are the two bilaterally symmetric AIA interneurons.
claims.source: The AIA-neuron reporter nIs843[Pgcy-28.d::mCherry] showed complete overlap with misexpressed Pceh-28::gfp, indicating that the cells misexpressing the M4 reporter are the two bilaterally symmetric and embryonically-generated AIA interneurons (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization experiments shown in Figure 1B demonstrating overlap between the AIA marker and misexpressed Pceh-28::gfp.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutants rarely misexpress Pceh-28::gfp at early larval stages, but display an increasing penetrance of this defect as worms transition through larval development.
claims.source: ctbp-1 mutants rarely misexpressed Pceh-28::gfp at early larval stages, but displayed an increasing penetrance, though invariant expressivity, of this defect as worms transitioned through larval development, such that by the last larval stage (L4) nearly all worms exhibited reporter misexpression specifically and solely in the AIAs (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1E showing the percentage of worms with AIA misexpression increases from L1 to L4 stages.

claims.claim: By the L4 larval stage, nearly all ctbp-1 mutant worms exhibit Pceh-28::gfp misexpression specifically and solely in the AIAs.
claims.source: ctbp-1 mutants rarely misexpressed Pceh-28::gfp at early larval stages, but displayed an increasing penetrance, though invariant expressivity, of this defect as worms transitioned through larval development, such that by the last larval stage (L4) nearly all worms exhibited reporter misexpression specifically and solely in the AIAs (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1E showing approximately 95% of L4 worms express the reporter in AIAs.

claims.claim: AIA-specific restoration of ctbp-1 is sufficient to suppress Pceh-28::gfp misexpression in an otherwise ctbp-1 mutant background.
claims.source: We found that AIA-specific restoration of ctbp-1 was sufficient to suppress Pceh-28::gfp misexpression in an otherwise ctbp-1 mutant background (Figure 1F; quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), demonstrating that ctbp-1 is able to act cell-autonomously to regulate ceh-28 expression in the AIA neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1F demonstrating that AIA-specific ctbp-1 expression prevents misexpression.

claims.claim: Heat shock during the L4 larval stage is sufficient to suppress Pceh-28::gfp misexpression in adult ctbp-1 mutant AIAs.
claims.source: We found that heat shock during the L4 larval stage was sufficient to suppress Pceh-28::gfp misexpression in adult ctbp-1 mutant AIAs (Figure 1G–H; quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), demonstrating that ctbp-1 can act in L4-to-young adult stage worms to regulate AIA gene expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by heat shock experiments shown in Figure 1G-H demonstrating rescue of misexpression when ctbp-1 is induced at L4.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant AIAs express all five of five AIA markers tested.
claims.source: We found that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs expressed all five of five AIA markers tested and did not express any of four other (non-ceh-28) M4 markers tested.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant AIAs do not express any of four other (non-ceh-28) M4 markers tested.
claims.source: We found that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs expressed all five of five AIA markers tested and did not express any of four other (non-ceh-28) M4 markers tested.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant AIAs do not misexpress either of the two tested M4 genes known to be directly regulated by ceh-28 (dbl-1 and egl-17).
claims.source: Of particular note, ctbp-1 mutant AIAs did not misexpress either of the two tested M4 genes known to be directly regulated by ceh-28 (i.e. dbl-1 and egl-17), indicating that the ceh-28 misexpression in mutant AIAs does not activate the ceh-28 regulatory pathway (Ramakrishnan and Okkema, 2014; Ramakrishnan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, along with citations to prior work on ceh-28 targets.

claims.claim: The ceh-28 misexpression in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs does not activate the ceh-28 regulatory pathway.
claims.source: Of particular note, ctbp-1 mutant AIAs did not misexpress either of the two tested M4 genes known to be directly regulated by ceh-28 (i.e. dbl-1 and egl-17), indicating that the ceh-28 misexpression in mutant AIAs does not activate the ceh-28 regulatory pathway (Ramakrishnan and Okkema, 2014; Ramakrishnan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that downstream targets of ceh-28 are not expressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs despite ceh-28 misexpression.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant AIAs are not transdifferentiated into M4-like cells.
claims.source: We conclude that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs are not transdifferentiated into M4-like cells and instead seem to retain much of their AIA identity while gaining at least one M4 characteristic (i.e. ceh-28 expression) later in life.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs express AIA markers but not M4 markers (except ceh-28).

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant AIAs retain much of their AIA identity while gaining at least one M4 characteristic (ceh-28 expression) later in life.
claims.source: We conclude that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs are not transdifferentiated into M4-like cells and instead seem to retain much of their AIA identity while gaining at least one M4 characteristic (i.e. ceh-28 expression) later in life.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs express AIA markers and ceh-28 but not other M4 markers.

claims.claim: L1 ctbp-1 mutant AIAs appear grossly wild-type in morphology.
claims.source: We found that L1 ctbp-1 mutant AIAs appeared grossly wild-type in morphology (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images in Figure 3A showing L1 ctbp-1 mutant AIAs with normal morphology.

claims.claim: L4 and adult ctbp-1 mutant AIAs have ectopic neurite branches that extend from both the anterior and posterior ends of the AIA cell body.
claims.source: However, L4 and adult ctbp-1 mutant AIAs had ectopic neurite branches that extended from both the anterior and posterior ends of the AIA cell body (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images in Figure 3A showing ectopic neurites in L4 and adult ctbp-1 mutant AIAs.

claims.claim: The penetrance of ectopic neurite branches in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs increases progressively in later larval stage and adult mutants.
claims.source: The penetrance of these ectopic branches increased progressively in later larval stage and adult mutants (Figure 3B–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 3B-C showing increasing percentages of AIAs with ectopic neurites from L1 to L4 to adult stages.

claims.claim: L4 and adult ctbp-1 mutant AIA cell bodies are significantly longer than their wild-type counterparts.
claims.source: Quantification of this defect revealed that L4 and adult mutant AIA cell bodies, but not those of L1s, were significantly longer than their wild-type counterparts (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3D demonstrating significantly increased AIA cell body length in L4 and adult ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: The maximum area of the AIA cell body does not significantly differ between wild-type and ctbp-1 mutant AIAs at any stage.
claims.source: We found that the maximum area of the AIA cell body did not significantly differ between wild-type and mutant AIAs at any stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that mutant AIAs were misshapen but not enlarged.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing no significant difference in AIA cell body area.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant AIAs are misshapen but not enlarged.
claims.source: We found that the maximum area of the AIA cell body did not significantly differ between wild-type and mutant AIAs at any stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that mutant AIAs were misshapen but not enlarged.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AIA cell bodies are longer but not larger in area, suggesting a change in shape rather than size.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 is not required for the establishment of proper AIA morphology but instead acts to maintain AIA morphology over time.
claims.source: Furthermore, the relative lack of AIA morphological defects in L1 ctbp-1 mutants suggests that ctbp-1 is not required for the establishment of proper AIA morphology but instead acts to maintain AIA morphology over time.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that L1 ctbp-1 mutant AIAs have normal morphology while L4 and adult mutants have morphological defects.

claims.claim: AIA-specific restoration of ctbp-1 in mutant worms rescues all AIA morphological defects to near-wild-type levels at all stages tested.
claims.source: We found that AIA-specific restoration of ctbp-1 in mutant worms rescued all AIA morphological defects to near-wild-type levels at all stages tested, indicating that ctbp-1 can act cell-autonomously to regulate AIA morphology (Figure 3F–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3F-H demonstrating that AIA-specific ctbp-1 expression restores normal AIA morphology.

claims.claim: Heat shock at the L4 stage does not restore ctbp-1 mutant AIA morphology in day 1 adults back to wild type.
claims.source: We found that heat shock at the L4 stage did not restore ctbp-1 mutant AIA morphology in day 1 adults back to wild type.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by heat shock experiments shown in Figure 3I-L demonstrating that late-stage induction of ctbp-1 does not fully rescue morphological defects.

claims.claim: Brief restoration of wild-type ctbp-1 activity is not able to restore mutant AIA morphology.
claims.source: While heat-shocked adults did display a lower frequency of morphological defects than did their non-heat-shocked counterparts, these differences were not significant, suggesting that brief restoration of wild-type ctbp-1 activity is not able to restore mutant AIA morphology (Figure 3I–L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by heat shock experiments shown in Figure 3I-L demonstrating that late-stage induction of ctbp-1 does not significantly rescue morphological defects.

claims.claim: The AIAs function in response to volatile odors and play an important role in learning associated with the sensation of volatile odors or salts.
claims.source: The AIAs function in response to volatile odors and play an important role in learning associated with the sensation of volatile odors or salts (Tomioka et al., 2006; Cho et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on AIA function.

claims.claim: Worms that had been briefly starved with 90 minutes of food deprivation and had no prior experience with butanone (naïve worms) are generally attracted to the odor.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies (Cho et al., 2016), we found that worms that had been briefly starved with 90 minutes of food deprivation and had no prior experience with butanone (so-called 'naïve' worms) were generally attracted to the odor, while worms that were briefly starved in the presence of butanone ('conditioned' worms) adapted to the odor and exhibited mild repulsion to it (Figure 4A–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A-E and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Worms that were briefly starved in the presence of butanone (conditioned worms) adapt to the odor and exhibit mild repulsion to it.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies (Cho et al., 2016), we found that worms that had been briefly starved with 90 minutes of food deprivation and had no prior experience with butanone (so-called 'naïve' worms) were generally attracted to the odor, while worms that were briefly starved in the presence of butanone ('conditioned' worms) adapted to the odor and exhibited mild repulsion to it (Figure 4A–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A-E and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: L1 ctbp-1 mutant worms show an ability to adapt to butanone roughly similar to that of their wild-type counterparts.
claims.source: We found that while L1 ctbp-1 worms showed an ability to adapt to butanone roughly similar to that of their wild-type counterparts, conditioned L4 ctbp-1 mutants displayed a significant decrease in repulsion from butanone relative to wild-type L4 animals, indicating a decrease in their ability to adapt to the odor (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4B-C demonstrating similar adaptation in L1 wild-type and ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Conditioned L4 ctbp-1 mutants display a significant decrease in repulsion from butanone relative to wild-type L4 animals, indicating a decrease in their ability to adapt to the odor.
claims.source: We found that while L1 ctbp-1 worms showed an ability to adapt to butanone roughly similar to that of their wild-type counterparts, conditioned L4 ctbp-1 mutants displayed a significant decrease in repulsion from butanone relative to wild-type L4 animals, indicating a decrease in their ability to adapt to the odor (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4D-E demonstrating reduced adaptation in L4 ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: AIA-ablated strain JN580 worms display decreased butanone adaptation at both the L1 and L4 larval stages.
claims.source: As a control, we assayed a strain carrying a transgenic construct that genetically ablates the AIA neurons, JN580. As expected, JN580 worms displayed decreased butanone adaptation at both the L1 and L4 larval stages.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4B-E demonstrating reduced adaptation in JN580 worms at both stages.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant worms display a defect in butanone adaptation similar to that of an AIA-ablated strain.
claims.source: Thus, ctbp-1 mutant worms displayed a defect in butanone adaptation similar to that of an AIA-ablated strain and did so only at a later larval stage, suggesting a potential loss of AIA function in L4 ctbp-1 mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4B-E comparing ctbp-1 mutants and AIA-ablated worms.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant L4 worms exhibit weaker butanone adaptation than their wild-type counterparts, but this defect is not as severe as that of JN580 L4s.
claims.source: However, while ctbp-1 mutant L4s exhibited weaker butanone adaptation than their wild-type counterparts, this defect was not as severe as that of JN580 L4s, indicating that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs might retain some function.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4D-E comparing wild-type, ctbp-1 mutant, and JN580 worms.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant AIAs might retain some function.
claims.source: However, while ctbp-1 mutant L4s exhibited weaker butanone adaptation than their wild-type counterparts, this defect was not as severe as that of JN580 L4s, indicating that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs might retain some function.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ctbp-1 mutants have a less severe adaptation defect than AIA-ablated worms.

claims.claim: The lack of a butanone adaptation defect in L1 ctbp-1 mutants shows that ctbp-1 is not required for the establishment of functional AIA neurons.
claims.source: Additionally, the lack of a butanone adaptation defect in L1 ctbp-1 mutants similar to that of L1 JN580 worms further suggests that loss of ctbp-1 does not disrupt early AIA function and shows that ctbp-1 is not required for the establishment of functional AIA neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that L1 ctbp-1 mutants have normal butanone adaptation while L4 mutants have defects.

claims.claim: AIA-specific restoration of ctbp-1 rescues butanone adaptation of conditioned ctbp-1 mutant L4s to near wild-type levels.
claims.source: We assayed ctbp-1 mutants carrying the AIA-specific rescue construct nIs743[PAIA::ctbp-1(+)] for butanone adaptation (Figure 4B–E) and found that AIA-specific restoration of ctbp-1 rescued butanone adaption of conditioned ctbp-1 mutant L4s to near wild-type levels (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4E demonstrating that AIA-specific ctbp-1 expression restores normal butanone adaptation.

claims.claim: The butanone adaptation defect of ctbp-1 mutants is caused by a disruption of AIA function.
claims.source: We conclude that the butanone adaptation defect of ctbp-1 mutants is caused by a disruption of AIA function and that ctbp-1 can act cell-autonomously to regulate this AIA function.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AIA-specific rescue of ctbp-1 restores normal butanone adaptation.

claims.claim: Restoration of ctbp-1 by heat shock at the L4 larval stage rescues the butanone adaptation defect in day one adults.
claims.source: Next, we assayed ctbp-1 mutants carrying the heat shock-inducible ctbp-1(+) rescue construct nEx2351[Phsp::ctbp-1(+)] for butanone adaptation. We found that restoration of ctbp-1 by heat shock at the L4 larval stage rescued the butanone adaptation defect in day one adults, indicating that ctbp-1 can act in L4-to-day 1 adult worms to maintain proper AIA function after the initial establishment of the AIA cell identity (Figure 4F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by heat shock experiments shown in Figure 4F-G demonstrating that late-stage induction of ctbp-1 restores normal butanone adaptation.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 can act in L4-to-day 1 adult worms to maintain proper AIA function after the initial establishment of the AIA cell identity.
claims.source: Next, we assayed ctbp-1 mutants carrying the heat shock-inducible ctbp-1(+) rescue construct nEx2351[Phsp::ctbp-1(+)] for butanone adaptation. We found that restoration of ctbp-1 by heat shock at the L4 larval stage rescued the butanone adaptation defect in day one adults, indicating that ctbp-1 can act in L4-to-day 1 adult worms to maintain proper AIA function after the initial establishment of the AIA cell identity (Figure 4F–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that late-stage induction of ctbp-1 restores normal butanone adaptation.

claims.claim: Naïve ctbp-1 mutant worms display a mildly weaker attraction to butanone than their wild-type counterparts at both the L1 and L4 larval stages.
claims.source: While conducting these assays, we observed that naïve ctbp-1 mutant worms displayed a mildly weaker attraction to butanone than did their wild-type counterparts at both the L1 and L4 larval stages (Figure 4B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4B and D demonstrating reduced attraction in naïve ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: AIA-specific rescue of ctbp-1 does not rescue the mild chemotaxis defect in naïve ctbp-1 mutants.
claims.source: AIA-specific rescue of ctbp-1 did not rescue this mild chemotaxis defect – naïve ctbp-1 mutants carrying the PAIA::ctbp-1(+) construct still displayed weaker butanone attraction than wild-type worms (Figure 4B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4B and D demonstrating that AIA-specific ctbp-1 expression does not restore normal attraction in naïve worms.

claims.claim: The defect in attraction to butanone in naïve ctbp-1 mutants is not a consequence of dysfunction of the AIAs but rather of some other cell(s) involved in butanone chemotaxis.
claims.source: We suggest that this defect in attraction to butanone is not a consequence of dysfunction of the AIAs but rather of some other cell(s) involved in butanone chemotaxis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that AIA-specific rescue does not restore normal attraction in naïve worms.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutants are defective in chemotaxis to the volatile odor isoamyl alcohol but not defective in the response to diacetyl.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that ctbp-1 mutants were defective in chemotaxis to the volatile odor isoamyl alcohol but were not defective in the response to diacetyl (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B) while AIA-ablated strain JN580 animals were not defective in either response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B demonstrating defects in isoamyl alcohol but not diacetyl chemotaxis.

claims.claim: AIA-ablated strain JN580 animals are not defective in chemotaxis to either diacetyl or isoamyl alcohol.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that ctbp-1 mutants were defective in chemotaxis to the volatile odor isoamyl alcohol but were not defective in the response to diacetyl (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B) while AIA-ablated strain JN580 animals were not defective in either response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by chemotaxis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B demonstrating normal chemotaxis in JN580 worms.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant worms have a broader defect in chemotaxis caused by the disruption of the function of cells other than the AIAs.
claims.source: These observations indicate that ctbp-1 mutant worms have a broader defect in chemotaxis caused by the disruption of the function of cells other than the AIAs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ctbp-1 mutants have chemotaxis defects that are not present in AIA-ablated worms and are not rescued by AIA-specific ctbp-1 expression.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 mutant AIAs show high levels of expression of ceh-28, while wild-type AIAs show no detectable ceh-28 expression.
claims.source: Confirming that these data captured changes in the AIA transcriptional profiles, we found that ctbp-1 mutant AIAs showed high levels of expression of ceh-28, while wild-type AIAs showed no detectable ceh-28 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: acbp-6 is not expressed in wild-type AIAs but is misexpressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs.
claims.source: We identified and confirmed one gene that, similar to ceh-28, was not expressed in wild-type AIAs but was misexpressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs: acbp-6, which is predicted to encode an acyl-Coenzyme A binding protein (Shaye and Greenwald, 2011; Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5A-B and single-cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: acbp-6 is predicted to encode an acyl-Coenzyme A binding protein.
claims.source: We identified and confirmed one gene that, similar to ceh-28, was not expressed in wild-type AIAs but was misexpressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs: acbp-6, which is predicted to encode an acyl-Coenzyme A binding protein (Shaye and Greenwald, 2011; Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on acbp-6.

claims.claim: sra-11 is expressed in wild-type AIAs but not expressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs.
claims.source: We also identified and confirmed two genes expressed in wild-type AIAs but not expressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs: sra-11, which encodes a transmembrane serpentine receptor (Troemel et al., 1995); and glr-2, which encodes a glutamate receptor (Brockie et al., 2001; Figure 5C and E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5C-D and single-cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: sra-11 encodes a transmembrane serpentine receptor.
claims.source: We also identified and confirmed two genes expressed in wild-type AIAs but not expressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs: sra-11, which encodes a transmembrane serpentine receptor (Troemel et al., 1995); and glr-2, which encodes a glutamate receptor (Brockie et al., 2001; Figure 5C and E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on sra-11.

claims.claim: glr-2 is expressed in wild-type AIAs but not expressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs.
claims.source: We also identified and confirmed two genes expressed in wild-type AIAs but not expressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs: sra-11, which encodes a transmembrane serpentine receptor (Troemel et al., 1995); and glr-2, which encodes a glutamate receptor (Brockie et al., 2001; Figure 5C and E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5E-F and single-cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: glr-2 encodes a glutamate receptor.
claims.source: We also identified and confirmed two genes expressed in wild-type AIAs but not expressed in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs: sra-11, which encodes a transmembrane serpentine receptor (Troemel et al., 1995); and glr-2, which encodes a glutamate receptor (Brockie et al., 2001; Figure 5C and E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on glr-2.

claims.claim: Pacbp-6::gfp is rarely detectable in the AIAs of either wild-type or ctbp-1 AIAs at the L1 stage but is consistently expressed in ctbp-1 mutant L4 AIAs.
claims.source: We also visualized these reporters in L1 wild-type and ctbp-1 worms and found that both Pacbp-6::gfp and Psra-11::gfp displayed a time-dependence to their expression similar to that of Pceh-28::gfp − Pacbp-6::gfp was rarely detectible in the AIAs of either wild-type or ctbp-1 AIAs at the L1 stage but was consistently expressed in ctbp-1 mutant L4 AIAs (Figure 5A–B), while Psra-11::gfp was rarely detectible in the AIAs of either wild-type or ctbp-1 mutant L1 worms but was expressed in the AIAs of most wild-type worms by the L4 stage while remaining off in the AIAs of most L4 ctbp-1 mutants (Figure 5C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5A-B demonstrating stage-dependent expression of Pacbp-6::gfp.

claims.claim: Psra-11::gfp is rarely detectable in the AIAs of either wild-type or ctbp-1 mutant L1 worms but is expressed in the AIAs of most wild-type worms by the L4 stage while remaining off in the AIAs of most L4 ctbp-1 mutants.
claims.source: We also visualized these reporters in L1 wild-type and ctbp-1 worms and found that both Pacbp-6::gfp and Psra-11::gfp displayed a time-dependence to their expression similar to that of Pceh-28::gfp − Pacbp-6::gfp was rarely detectible in the AIAs of either wild-type or ctbp-1 AIAs at the L1 stage but was consistently expressed in ctbp-1 mutant L4 AIAs (Figure 5A–B), while Psra-11::gfp was rarely detectible in the AIAs of either wild-type or ctbp-1 mutant L1 worms but was expressed in the AIAs of most wild-type worms by the L4 stage while remaining off in the AIAs of most L4 ctbp-1 mutants (Figure 5C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5C-D demonstrating stage-dependent expression of Psra-11::gfp.

claims.claim: acbp-6 and sra-11 expression is regulated by ctbp-1 primarily in the AIAs of late-stage larvae and adults.
claims.source: These observations suggest that, like ceh-28 expression, acbp-6 and sra-11 expression is regulated by ctbp-1 primarily in the AIAs of late-stage larvae and adults.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that acbp-6 and sra-11 expression changes occur primarily at later larval stages.

claims.claim: glr-2 is expressed in wild-type but not ctbp-1 AIAs in both L1 and L4 larvae.
claims.source: By contrast, glr-2 was expressed in wild-type but not ctbp-1 AIAs in both L1 and L4 larvae (Figure 5E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5E-F demonstrating glr-2 expression at both L1 and L4 stages.

claims.claim: Mutant AIAs fail to turn on and/or maintain the expression of genes characteristic of the adult AIA neuron (sra-11 and glr-2) while misexpressing at least two genes uncharacteristic of AIA (ceh-28 and acbp-6).
claims.source: These data demonstrate that mutant AIAs fail to turn on and/or maintain the expression of genes characteristic of the adult AIA neuron (sra-11 and glr-2) while misexpressing at least two genes uncharacteristic of AIA (ceh-28 and acbp-6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5 demonstrating changes in gene expression in ctbp-1 mutant AIAs.

claims.claim: The majority of abnormalities in AIA gene expression occur long after the AIAs are generated during embryogenesis.
claims.source: That the majority of these abnormalities in AIA gene expression occurred long after the AIAs are generated during embryogenesis further supports the conclusion that ctbp-1 does not act to establish the AIA cell identity.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most gene expression changes occur at later larval stages rather than at L1.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 acts to maintain the AIA cell identity, plays little to no role in the initial establishment of the AIA cell fate, and can act cell-autonomously and in older worms to maintain these aspects of the AIA identity.
claims.source: Collectively, our findings concerning AIA gene expression, morphology and function demonstrate that ctbp-1 acts to maintain the AIA cell identity, plays little to no role in the initial establishment of the AIA cell fate, and can act cell-autonomously and in older worms to maintain these aspects of the AIA identity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data throughout the manuscript showing that ctbp-1 defects appear at later stages, can be rescued by AIA-specific expression, and can be rescued by late-stage induction.

claims.claim: Three alleles of egl-13 were isolated as ctbp-1 suppressors: n5937, n6013, and n6313.
claims.source: We isolated three alleles of egl-13 as ctbp-1 suppressors: n5937, a mutation of the splice acceptor site at the beginning of the 6th exon of the egl-13a isoform resulting in a frameshift and early stop; n6013, a Q381ochre nonsense mutation toward the end of the egl-13 transcript; and n6313, a 436-nucleotide deletion spanning the 7th and 8th exons of the egl-13a isoform (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic screen data and sequencing results shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: A transgenic construct carrying a wild-type copy of egl-13 under its native promoter rescues the suppression of Pceh-28::gfp misexpression by all three egl-13 alleles.
claims.source: We generated and introduced a transgenic construct carrying a wild-type copy of egl-13 under its native promoter into these mutant strains and found that this construct was capable of rescuing the suppression of Pceh-28::gfp misexpression by all three egl-13 alleles, demonstrating that loss of egl-13 function suppresses this aspect of the ctbp-1 mutant phenotype and suggesting that these alleles are likely loss-of-function alleles of egl-13 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C demonstrating that wild-type egl-13 restores the ctbp-1 mutant phenotype.

claims.claim: Loss of egl-13 function suppresses Pceh-28::gfp misexpression in ctbp-1 mutants.
claims.source: We generated and introduced a transgenic construct carrying a wild-type copy of egl-13 under its native promoter into these mutant strains and found that this construct was capable of rescuing the suppression of Pceh-28::gfp misexpression by all three egl-13 alleles, demonstrating that loss of egl-13 function suppresses this aspect of the ctbp-1 mutant phenotype and suggesting that these alleles are likely loss-of-function alleles of egl-13 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic suppression data shown in Figure 6D and rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: egl-13 has been shown to act in the establishment of the BAG and URX cell fates and in vulval development of C. elegans.
claims.source: egl-13 has been shown to act in the establishment of the BAG and URX cell fates and in vulval development of C. elegans (Gramstrup Petersen et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013), and its mammalian orthologs SOX5 and SOX6 act in neural fate determination (Ji and Kim, 2016; Saleem et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on egl-13 function.

claims.claim: The mammalian orthologs of egl-13, SOX5 and SOX6, act in neural fate determination.
claims.source: egl-13 has been shown to act in the establishment of the BAG and URX cell fates and in vulval development of C. elegans (Gramstrup Petersen et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013), and its mammalian orthologs SOX5 and SOX6 act in neural fate determination (Ji and Kim, 2016; Saleem et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on SOX5 and SOX6 function.

claims.claim: ttx-3 is a LIM homeobox transcription factor characterized for its roles in thermotaxis behavior and in cell-fate specification of the AIA and AIY interneurons.
claims.source: ttx-3 is a LIM homeobox transcription factor characterized for its roles in thermotaxis behavior and in cell-fate specification of the AIA and AIY interneurons (Altun-Gultekin et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on ttx-3 function.

claims.claim: The TTX-3 mammalian ortholog LHX9 is involved in retinal cell-fate establishment.
claims.source: The TTX-3 mammalian ortholog LHX9 is involved in retinal cell-fate establishment (Balasubramanian et al., 2014; Balasubramanian et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on LHX9 function.

claims.claim: Two alleles of ttx-3 were isolated: the nonsense allele n6308 and the missense allele n6316.
claims.source: We isolated two alleles of ttx-3: the nonsense allele n6308 and the missense allele n6316 (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic screen data and sequencing results shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: Two additional ttx-3 alleles, the splice acceptor allele ks5 and the Q303amber nonsense allele ot22, suppress ctbp-1-driven nIs175 misexpression.
claims.source: We tested two additional ttx-3 alleles, the splice acceptor allele ks5 and the Q303amber nonsense allele ot22. Both suppressed ctbp-1-driven nIs175 misexpression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic suppression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Suppression of ctbp-1 by either n6308 or n6316 is rescued by introduction of a transgenic construct carrying a wild-type copy of ttx-3 expressed under the control of its native promoter.
claims.source: Suppression of ctbp-1 by either of our isolated alleles (n6308 or n6316) was rescued by introduction of a transgenic construct carrying a wild-type copy of ttx-3 expressed under the control of its native promoter (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), indicating that these alleles are likely loss-of-function alleles that reduce or eliminate ttx-3 gene function.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C demonstrating that wild-type ttx-3 restores the ctbp-1 mutant phenotype.

claims.claim: egl-13(n5937) strongly suppresses ctbp-1 at all stages, resulting in little to no misexpression of Pceh-28::gfp in the AIAs of egl-13 ctbp-1 double mutants at any larval stage or in day 1 adults.
claims.source: egl-13(n5937) strongly suppressed ctbp-1 at all stages, resulting in little to no misexpression of Pceh-28::gfp in the AIAs of egl-13 ctbp-1 double mutants at any larval stage or in day 1 adults.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D demonstrating strong suppression by egl-13 mutation.

claims.claim: Suppression by ttx-3(n6308) is incompletely penetrant, showing a progressive increase in AIA gene misexpression that peaks at adulthood with approximately 45% of ctbp-1 ttx-3 double-mutant animals displaying Pceh-28::gfp expression in the AIAs.
claims.source: Suppression by ttx-3(n6308) was incompletely penetrant, showing a progressive increase in AIA gene misexpression that peaked at adulthood with approximately 45% of ctbp-1 ttx-3 double-mutant animals displaying Pceh-28::gfp expression in the AIAs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D demonstrating partial suppression by ttx-3 mutation.

claims.claim: Loss of egl-13 has little consistent effect on the AIA morphological defects caused by a loss of ctbp-1 activity.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that loss of egl-13 has little consistent effect on the AIA morphological defects caused by a loss of ctbp-1 activity, suggesting that ctbp-1 maintains AIA morphology primarily through egl-13-independent pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 6E-H demonstrating that egl-13 mutation does not significantly rescue morphological defects.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 maintains AIA morphology primarily through egl-13-independent pathways.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that loss of egl-13 has little consistent effect on the AIA morphological defects caused by a loss of ctbp-1 activity, suggesting that ctbp-1 maintains AIA morphology primarily through egl-13-independent pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that egl-13 mutation does not significantly rescue morphological defects in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: The additional loss of ttx-3 results in less severe morphological abnormalities than occurs in ctbp-1 single mutants.
claims.source: These data further indicate that the additional loss of ttx-3 results in less severe morphological abnormalities than occurs in ctbp-1 single mutants, suggesting that the manifestation of AIA morphological defects seen in ctbp-1 single mutants likely rely in part on proper ttx-3 activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 6E-H demonstrating that ttx-3 mutation partially suppresses morphological defects.

claims.claim: The manifestation of AIA morphological defects seen in ctbp-1 single mutants likely relies in part on proper ttx-3 activity.
claims.source: These data further indicate that the additional loss of ttx-3 results in less severe morphological abnormalities than occurs in ctbp-1 single mutants, suggesting that the manifestation of AIA morphological defects seen in ctbp-1 single mutants likely rely in part on proper ttx-3 activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ttx-3 mutation partially suppresses morphological defects in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: At the L1 larval stage, egl-13 ctbp-1 and ctbp-1 ttx-3 double mutant strains display a detectable response to butanone similar to ctbp-1 single mutants.
claims.source: We tested egl-13 ctbp-1 and ctbp-1 ttx-3 double mutants for butanone adaptation and found that, at the L1 larval stage, these double mutant strains displayed a detectable response to butanone similar to ctbp-1 single mutants (Figure 6I–J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 6I-J demonstrating similar butanone responses in L1 double mutants and ctbp-1 single mutants.

claims.claim: At the L4 larval stage, mutation of egl-13 strongly suppresses the ctbp-1 mutant defect in butanone adaptation, causing near wild-type levels of repulsion in conditioned worms.
claims.source: At the L4 larval stage, mutation of egl-13 strongly suppressed the ctbp-1 mutant defect in butanone adaptation, causing near wild-type levels of repulsion in conditioned worms (Figure 6K–L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 6K-L demonstrating that egl-13 mutation restores normal butanone adaptation in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: At the L4 stage, mutation of ttx-3 fails to suppress AIA functional defects and instead shows an even greater defect in butanone adaptation than ctbp-1 single mutants.
claims.source: By contrast, at the L4 stage mutation of ttx-3 failed to suppress AIA functional defects and instead showed an even greater defect in butanone adaption than did ctbp-1 single mutants (Figure 6K–L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 6K-L demonstrating that ttx-3 mutation exacerbates the butanone adaptation defect in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Loss of egl-13 activity suppresses AIA functional defects of ctbp-1 mutant worms.
claims.source: These results indicate that loss of egl-13 activity suppressed AIA functional defects of ctbp-1 mutant worms and suggest that ctbp-1 maintains at least this aspect of AIA cellular function primarily through an egl-13-dependent pathway, while loss of ttx-3 exacerbates the AIA functional defect seen in ctbp-1 single mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 6K-L demonstrating that egl-13 mutation restores normal butanone adaptation in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 maintains at least some aspects of AIA cellular function primarily through an egl-13-dependent pathway.
claims.source: These results indicate that loss of egl-13 activity suppressed AIA functional defects of ctbp-1 mutant worms and suggest that ctbp-1 maintains at least this aspect of AIA cellular function primarily through an egl-13-dependent pathway, while loss of ttx-3 exacerbates the AIA functional defect seen in ctbp-1 single mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that egl-13 mutation suppresses AIA functional defects in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 maintains AIA function and at least some aspects of AIA gene expression through egl-13.
claims.source: From these data, we conclude that ctbp-1 maintains AIA function and at least some aspects of AIA gene expression through egl-13 and that disruptions to AIA morphology appears to be controlled independently of egl-13 function.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic suppression data showing that egl-13 mutation suppresses AIA functional defects and some gene expression defects in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Disruptions to AIA morphology appear to be controlled independently of egl-13 function.
claims.source: From these data, we conclude that ctbp-1 maintains AIA function and at least some aspects of AIA gene expression through egl-13 and that disruptions to AIA morphology appears to be controlled independently of egl-13 function.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that egl-13 mutation does not significantly rescue morphological defects in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Loss of ttx-3 similarly restores at least some aspects of AIA gene expression as well as partially suppresses AIA morphological defects seen in ctbp-1 single mutants.
claims.source: We further conclude that loss of ttx-3 similarly restores at least some aspects of AIA gene expression as well as partially suppresses AIA morphological defects seen in ctbp-1 single mutants, while AIA function seems to be further perturbed in the absence of ttx-3.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic suppression data showing that ttx-3 mutation suppresses some gene expression defects and partially suppresses morphological defects in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: AIA function seems to be further perturbed in the absence of ttx-3.
claims.source: We further conclude that loss of ttx-3 similarly restores at least some aspects of AIA gene expression as well as partially suppresses AIA morphological defects seen in ctbp-1 single mutants, while AIA function seems to be further perturbed in the absence of ttx-3.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data showing that ttx-3 mutation exacerbates the butanone adaptation defect in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Mutation of ctbp-1 does not affect ttx-3 expression in the AIAs.
claims.source: Mutation of ctbp-1 does not affect ttx-3 expression in the AIAs (Figure 2B), suggesting that the AIA identity defects that characterize ctbp-1 single mutants are not a consequence of a change in ttx-3 expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating that ttx-3 expression is unchanged in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: The AIA identity defects that characterize ctbp-1 single mutants are not a consequence of a change in ttx-3 expression.
claims.source: Mutation of ctbp-1 does not affect ttx-3 expression in the AIAs (Figure 2B), suggesting that the AIA identity defects that characterize ctbp-1 single mutants are not a consequence of a change in ttx-3 expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ttx-3 expression is unchanged in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Mutation of ttx-3 appears to suppress AIA cell-identity maintenance defects caused by a loss of ctbp-1 by perturbing AIA cell-identity establishment.
claims.source: Given ttx-3's known requirement as an AIA terminal selector (Zhang et al., 2014), we speculate that mutation of ttx-3 appears to suppress AIA cell-identity maintenance defects caused by a loss of ctbp-1 by perturbing AIA cell-identity establishment.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the known role of ttx-3 in AIA cell-fate specification and the observation that ttx-3 mutation suppresses some ctbp-1 phenotypes.

claims.claim: Failure to properly establish the AIA cell identity, as likely occurs in ttx-3 mutants, masks defects caused by the loss of the maintenance of that cell identity, as occurs in ctbp-1 mutants.
claims.source: In other words, failure to properly establish the AIA cell identity, as likely occurs in ttx-3 mutants, masks defects caused by the loss of the maintenance of that cell identity, as occurs in ctbp-1 mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that ttx-3 mutation suppresses some ctbp-1 phenotypes.

claims.claim: egl-13 can function cell-autonomously in the AIAs.
claims.source: Introduction of this construct to egl-13(n5937) ctbp-1 double mutants rescued the egl-13 suppression of Pceh-28::gfp misexpression in the AIAs, indicating that egl-13 can function cell-autonomously (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B demonstrating that AIA-specific egl-13 expression restores the ctbp-1 mutant phenotype.

claims.claim: egl-13 is expressed in a number of cells, including the AIAs, of wild-type worms.
claims.source: We further tested egl-13 expression using a GFP transcriptional reporter and found that egl-13 was expressed in a number of cells, including the AIAs, of wild-type worms (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), although expression in the AIAs appeared to dissipate over the course of larval development (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A demonstrating egl-13 expression in multiple cells including AIAs.

claims.claim: egl-13 expression in the AIAs appears to dissipate over the course of larval development.
claims.source: We further tested egl-13 expression using a GFP transcriptional reporter and found that egl-13 was expressed in a number of cells, including the AIAs, of wild-type worms (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), although expression in the AIAs appeared to dissipate over the course of larval development (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C demonstrating decreasing egl-13 expression in AIAs over time.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 does not appear to regulate egl-13 expression in the AIAs.
claims.source: We also tested the effect of mutation of ctbp-1 on egl-13 expression and found no significant difference between wild-type and ctbp-1 worms at any stage tested, indicating that ctbp-1 does not appear to regulate egl-13 expression in the AIAs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-C demonstrating no significant difference in egl-13 expression between wild-type and ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: In the absence of ctbp-1 function, ectopic egl-13 activity in the AIAs drives ceh-28 misexpression.
claims.source: These results suggest that, in the absence of ctbp-1 function, ectopic egl-13 activity in the AIAs drives ceh-28 misexpression, and thus that ctbp-1 likely normally acts to repress egl-13 activity in the AIAs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that egl-13 mutation suppresses ceh-28 misexpression in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: ctbp-1 likely normally acts to repress egl-13 activity in the AIAs.
claims.source: These results suggest that, in the absence of ctbp-1 function, ectopic egl-13 activity in the AIAs drives ceh-28 misexpression, and thus that ctbp-1 likely normally acts to repress egl-13 activity in the AIAs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that egl-13 mutation suppresses ceh-28 misexpression in ctbp-1 mutants and that ctbp-1 does not regulate egl-13 expression.

claims.claim: The mammalian CtBPs (CtBP1 and CtBP2) bind PXDLS-like motifs on a number of diverse transcription factors to target specific genetic loci for silencing.
claims.source: The mammalian CtBPs (CtBP1 and CtBP2) bind PXDLS-like motifs on a number of diverse transcription factors to target specific genetic loci for silencing (Chinnadurai, 2003; Shi et al., 2003; Stankiewicz et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on CtBP function.

claims.claim: The mammalian ortholog of EGL-13 (SOX6) interacts with the mammalian ortholog of CTBP-1 (CtBP2) through a PLNLS motif located in SOX6 to repress Fgf-3 expression in the developing mouse auditory otic vesicle.
claims.source: The mammalian ortholog of EGL-13 (SOX6) interacts with the mammalian ortholog of CTBP-1 (CtBP2) through a PLNLS motif located in SOX6 to repress Fgf-3 expression in the developing mouse auditory otic vesicle (Murakami et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on SOX6-CtBP2 interaction.

claims.claim: The PLNLS motif in SOX6 is 100% conserved in C. elegans EGL-13.
claims.source: This motif is 100% conserved in C. elegans EGL-13 and, since both CTBP-1 and EGL-13 can function cell-autonomously in the AIAs, we hypothesized that CTBP-1 and EGL-13 might physically interact.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison between SOX6 and EGL-13.

claims.claim: CTBP-1 and EGL-13 are able to physically interact in a yeast 2-hybrid assay.
claims.source: We performed a yeast 2-hybrid assay to test this hypothesis and found that CTBP-1 and EGL-13 are indeed able to physically interact in this assay (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by yeast 2-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating interaction between CTBP-1 and EGL-13.

claims.claim: A leucine-to-histidine mutation of the second leucine in the PLNLS motif (to PLNHS) disrupts the SOX6 – CtBP2 interaction, resulting in a mutant SOX6 protein that is unable to interact with CtBP2.
claims.source: These previous studies have further shown that the SOX6 – CtBP2 interaction can be disrupted by a leucine-to-histidine mutation of the second leucine in the PLNLS motif (to PLNHS), resulting in a mutant SOX6 protein that is unable to interact with CtBP2 (Murakami et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on SOX6-CtBP2 interaction.

claims.claim: An L259H mutation in EGL-13 disrupts its interaction with CTBP-1 in a yeast 2-hybrid assay.
claims.source: We generated a mutant EGL-13 variant bearing an L259H mutation, disrupting this motif, and found that this mutation disrupted its interaction with CTBP-1 in a yeast 2-hybrid assay (Figure 7B), suggesting that EGL-13's PLNLS motif is critical for the EGL-13 – CTBP-1 interaction.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by yeast 2-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 7B demonstrating that the L259H mutation disrupts the CTBP-1-EGL-13 interaction.

claims.claim: EGL-13's PLNLS motif is critical for the EGL-13 – CTBP-1 interaction.
claims.source: We generated a mutant EGL-13 variant bearing an L259H mutation, disrupting this motif, and found that this mutation disrupted its interaction with CTBP-1 in a yeast 2-hybrid assay (Figure 7B), suggesting that EGL-13's PLNLS motif is critical for the EGL-13 – CTBP-1 interaction.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the L259H mutation disrupts the CTBP-1-EGL-13 interaction in yeast 2-hybrid assays.

claims.claim: The L259H mutation in egl-13 does not induce Pceh-28::gfp misexpression at either the L1 or L4 larval stages in any of the worms scored.
claims.source: We found that this mutation did not induce reporter misexpression at either the L1 or L4 larval stages in any of the worms scored (Figure 7C; quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 3), indicating that disruption of the EGL-13 – CTBP-1 interaction alone in not sufficient to induce misexpression of ceh-28 in the AIAs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 7C and quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 3 demonstrating no misexpression in L259H mutants.

claims.claim: Disruption of the EGL-13 – CTBP-1 interaction alone is not sufficient to induce misexpression of ceh-28 in the AIAs.
claims.source: We found that this mutation did not induce reporter misexpression at either the L1 or L4 larval stages in any of the worms scored (Figure 7C; quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 3), indicating that disruption of the EGL-13 – CTBP-1 interaction alone in not sufficient to induce misexpression of ceh-28 in the AIAs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the L259H mutation does not cause ceh-28 misexpression in wild-type worms.

claims.claim: Mutation of egl-13 suppresses Pacbp-6::gfp misexpression in the AIAs of ctbp-1 mutants.
claims.source: We found that mutation of egl-13 suppressed Pacbp-6::gfp misexpression in the AIAs (Figure 8A and D, compare to Figure 5), just as egl-13 mutation suppressed Pceh-28::gfp misexpression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 8A and D demonstrating that egl-13 mutation prevents acbp-6 misexpression in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Mutation of egl-13 has no effect on the loss of Psra-11::gfp or Pglr-2::gfp expression in ctbp-1 mutants.
claims.source: By contrast, mutation of egl-13 had no effect on the loss of Psra-11::gfp or Pglr-2::gfp expression in ctbp-1 mutants (Figure 8B–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 8B-D demonstrating that egl-13 mutation does not restore sra-11 or glr-2 expression in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: Regulation of ceh-28 and acbp-6 by EGL-13 is likely indirect.
claims.source: We speculated that EGL-13 might directly regulate expression of ceh-28 or acbp-6. To test this hypothesis, we examined the ceh-28 and acbp-6 promoter regions for possible EGL-13 binding sites. We failed to identify any promising candidates, suggesting that regulation of these genes by EGL-13 is likely indirect.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the failure to identify EGL-13 binding sites in the ceh-28 and acbp-6 promoters.

claims.claim: Some, though not all, of the AIA gene expression defects seen in ctbp-1 mutants are regulated through egl-13.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that some, though not all, of the AIA gene expression defects seen in ctbp-1 mutants are regulated through egl-13.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that egl-13 mutation suppresses some gene expression defects (ceh-28, acbp-6) but not others (sra-11, glr-2) in ctbp-1 mutants.

claims.claim: acbp-6; ctbp-1 double mutants are nearly identical to both naïve and conditioned ctbp-1 single mutants at both the L1 and L4 larval stages.
claims.source: We found that acbp-6; ctbp-1 double mutants were nearly identical to both naïve and conditioned ctbp-1 single mutants at both the L1 and L4 larval stages (Figure 9A–D), indicating that misexpressed acbp-6 is likely not responsible for the observed AIA functional defect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 9A-D demonstrating similar butanone responses in acbp-6; ctbp-1 double mutants and ctbp-1 single mutants.
